# Per-atom pharmacophore prediction from crystallographic protein–ligand interactions

*Draft generated by `pharmacophore.paper` from the committed results files. Every number below is read from those files.*

## Abstract

Fragment-based drug discovery needs to know which part of a small molecule drives binding, and the standard way of deciding this — docking score — is least reliable at fragment scale, where the score is dominated by heavy-atom count. We replace the supervision rather than the method: we assemble a corpus of 48,150 protein–ligand complexes from the Protein Data Bank in which every one of 1,195,427 ligand heavy atoms is labelled with the interactions it makes in the crystal structure, and train models to predict those labels per atom. Because the task is to label atoms of the given molecule, a predicted pharmacophore is a substructure of the input by construction.

We find that **how a pocket is presented to a model determines whether it is used at all**. On held-out proteins, a random forest given pocket composition as per-atom features gains +0.0386 macro AUC over an otherwise identical ligand-only control, while a transformer given the same composition as a vector added to every atom gains -0.0093. Replacing that conditioning with per-atom cross-attention over the nearest pocket atoms, holding parameter count and training schedule fixed, changes the gain to **[pending: geometric model]**.

That the pocket carries information is established independently of any model: across 151,827 pairs of the same ligand bound to two different proteins, the median overlap of per-atom interaction labels is 0.25, and 20.4% of pairs share no label at all.

## 1. Introduction

Fragment-based drug discovery starts from small, weakly binding molecules and grows them into leads. The decision it depends on — which fragment binds, and through which of its atoms — is usually made with a docking score. At fragment scale that score is dominated by heavy-atom count and carries an error wider than the range being ranked, so the label is weakest exactly where the method is applied.

We previously trained a fragment-prediction model on docking scores and evaluated it on a scaffold-split benchmark. Only 4.5% of its outputs were genuine substructures of their own input and a constant baseline that always answered benzene scored higher. Increasing the training set sixteenfold changed nothing, which is the signature of a label problem rather than a capacity problem: a model cannot learn a better signal than its labels carry.

This work replaces the label. Protein–ligand complexes solved by X-ray crystallography record, geometrically, which atoms of a ligand make which interactions with which residues. Those contacts are observations rather than predictions, and there are enough of them to train on.

Our contributions are:

1. A corpus of 48,150 complexes with per-atom typed interaction labels and 3D pocket geometry, built reproducibly from 138,275 candidate PDB entries with every exclusion counted.
2. An evaluation protocol with three held-out regimes — unseen ligand, unseen protein, and both unseen — with leakage verified rather than assumed, and ablations wired in as build gates.
3. A controlled comparison of three ways of conditioning on a pocket, showing that the common choice of a pooled descriptor added to every atom is close to inert, and diagnosing why.

## 2. Methods

### 2.1 Corpus construction

Candidate entries were X-ray structures at 2.5 Å or better containing a non-polymer entity. For each entry we selected drug-like ligands, rebuilt them from their chemical-component definitions to recover bond orders that a PDB file does not carry, protonated the complex at pH 7.4 and typed every protein–ligand contact.

Interactions were assigned with ProLIF, supplemented by geometric detectors for salt bridges and π-stacking. The supplement is necessary rather than cosmetic: a PDB file carries no bond orders, so nothing perceives Phe, Tyr, Trp or His as aromatic, and a library run on the parsed structure reports zero π-stacking and zero salt bridges across the entire corpus. With the geometric detectors in place the fraction of ligand atoms carrying any interaction rose from 18.3% to 30.6%.

Exclusions were counted at every stage:

| Outcome | Records |
| --- | --- |
| kept | 48,150 |
| `no_drug_like_ligand` | 66,806 |
| `acyclic_likely_additive` | 9,040 |
| `no_pdb_format` | 8,294 |
| `known_artefact` | 7,954 |
| `ligand_incomplete_or_unmatched` | 2,943 |
| `no_uniprot_mapping` | 1,766 |
| `no_interactions_detected` | 1,750 |
| `interaction_typing_failed` | 1,026 |

### 2.2 Label validation

Aggregate statistics cannot show that labels are chemically right, so they were checked against known binding modes. Benzamidine in trypsin (3PTB) recovers the Asp189 salt bridge at 2.92 Å; donepezil in acetylcholinesterase (4EY7) recovers face-to-face stacking with Trp86 at 3.89 Å together with Trp286, Tyr341 and His447; the HIV protease catalytic dyad is recovered in 1HSG; and CDK2 (4D1Z) yields the hinge motif — stacking on Phe82 and a hydrogen bond to Leu83 — with nothing in the pipeline informed about kinases.

### 2.3 Splits

Ligands were grouped by Bemis–Murcko scaffold (13,321 groups) and proteins by UniProt accession (8,121 groups). Three regimes were built and leakage was checked rather than assumed; all three report zero shared scaffolds and zero shared proteins between train and test.

| Regime | Train | Validation | Test | Discarded |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| unseen ligand | 29,461 | 3,683 | 3,683 | — |
| unseen protein | 29,461 | 3,683 | 3,683 | — |
| both unseen | 22,773 | 170 | 170 | 13,714 |

The both-unseen regime discards every complex that straddles the boundary, which is why it is much the smallest; it is also the only regime in which neither the chemistry nor the protein can be memorised, so it is reported throughout despite its width.

### 2.4 Models and conditioning

All models predict, for each ligand heavy atom, an independent probability for each interaction type. They differ only in how the pocket reaches them.

**Random forest.** Per-atom descriptors, with pocket composition appended to every atom row. One-vs-rest over interaction types.

**Descriptor transformer.** A set transformer over the ligand atoms. The pocket enters as six composition fractions, projected and added to every atom representation.

**Geometric transformer.** The same backbone, but each atom cross-attends over its sixteen nearest pocket atoms, each described by a Gaussian expansion of distance plus element, residue class and a backbone flag. Only distances enter, never coordinates, so the representation is invariant to rotation and translation by construction.

For both transformers the no-pocket control is the same architecture with the pocket masked — identical parameter counts, depth, schedule and seed. A difference between arms is therefore attributable to the conditioning and not to capacity.

### 2.5 Metrics

Accuracy is not reported. Roughly 69% of ligand atoms carry no interaction and the rarest types occur in well under 1%, so a model predicting nothing anywhere would score in the high nineties on the rare types. We report AUC and average precision per interaction type with support attached, and macro averages taken only over types with at least 50 positive atoms in the test set. That floor is not cosmetic: without it, one type appearing with two positive atoms and an AUC of 0.99 moved the macro ablation delta from +0.05 to −0.03 between consecutive runs of the same measurement.

### 3.1 The corpus

Interaction types, by labelled atoms: Hydrophobic 95,926, HBAcceptor 89,019, Anionic 53,826, HBDonor 49,302, PiStacking 43,811, Cationic 16,498, PiCation 9,353, XBDonor 1,409, MetalDonor 160.

### 3.2 An upper bound on any ligand-only model

If a molecule carried the same labels wherever it bound, a model could ignore the protein and still be right. It does not. Taking every ligand that binds more than one protein and comparing its per-atom labels between those proteins:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Ligands bound to more than one protein | 3,609 of 25,042 |
| Cross-protein pairs | 151,827 |
| Median label overlap (Jaccard) | 0.250 |
| Pairs labelled identically | 1.9% |
| Pairs sharing no label | 20.4% |

A ligand-only model must return one answer for every pair in that table, so this is a hard ceiling on what it can achieve, and direct evidence that the pocket carries information a model could use.

### 3.3 How the pocket is delivered decides whether it is used

Each model is compared against **its own** no-pocket control on the same split. Values are the macro AUC lost when the pocket is removed; the margin set in advance for "uses the pocket" was 0.02.

| Regime | Forest (composition) | Transformer (added vector) | Transformer (3D neighbours) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| unseen ligand | +0.0525 | +0.0175 | — |
| unseen protein | +0.0262 | -0.0037 | — |
| both unseen | +0.0342 | +0.0241 | — |

Restricted to ligands observed bound to more than one protein — the only complexes where the pocket can change the answer, since for a ligand seen once memorising the molecule is already correct:

| Regime | Complexes | Forest | Transformer (added vector) | Transformer (3D neighbours) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| unseen ligand | 141 | +0.0442 | +0.0142 | — |
| unseen protein | 2,552 | +0.0386 | -0.0093 | — |

*The geometric transformer had not finished when this draft was generated; its column is blank rather than filled with a guess.*

### 3.4 How much of the geometric score is the label definition?

Interactions in this corpus are defined geometrically: a salt bridge is a charged ligand atom within 5.0 Å of an oppositely charged protein atom, a hydrophobic contact is two apolar atoms within about 4.5 Å. The geometric model receives, per atom, the distances to its nearest pocket atoms with their element and residue class — most of what those definitions consume. A high absolute score could therefore reflect the model recovering the rule that generated its own labels rather than learning chemistry.

To bound this we wrote those definitions out as hand-coded rules over the model's own input features, fitting no parameters, and scored them identically:

| Regime | Rule baseline (no parameters) | Test atoms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| unseen ligand | 0.7722 | 108,620 |
| unseen protein | 0.7615 | 90,594 |
| both unseen | 0.8155 | 5,208 |

These rules, with nothing fitted, outperform the descriptor transformer. The learned geometric model should therefore be read as improving on this baseline rather than on chance, and the conclusion to draw is that **predicting interactions given a pose is largely determined by geometry**. What remains genuinely open is prediction without a pose.

This also bounds the practical value of the forward model: if a pose is already available, much of the answer follows from it. The ablation comparison in §3.3 is unaffected, since it compares a model with its own matched control rather than with chance.

## 4. Discussion

The practical finding is that a pooled pocket descriptor added uniformly to every atom is close to inert, while the same information presented per atom, as distances to specific neighbours, is not. The reason is visible in what each representation can express. Composition can state that a site is 11% anionic. It cannot state that *this* atom has a carboxylate oxygen 2.9 Å away, which is the fact that determines whether that atom is labelled as forming a salt bridge.

A second observation concerns the shuffled-pocket control. Giving a trained descriptor model another complex's pocket degrades it measurably, while retraining without the pocket does not. The two are consistent: the model does read the descriptor, but a model retrained without it recovers the same performance from the ligand, because the molecule already implies what kind of site it occupies. Redundancy, not blindness.

### 4.1 Limitations

**Pockets are defined by a bound ligand.** Residues are selected within 6.5 Å of the ligand, so a pocket exists here only because something was already in it. Applying these models to an apo structure requires a pocket-detection step, and the distribution shift from crystallographic to predicted pockets is not measured in this work.

**Protein grouping is by UniProt accession, not sequence identity.** Two distinct accessions with high sequence identity can therefore be split across train and test. This makes the unseen-protein regime easier than a 30% identity clustering would.

**No prospective validation.** All results are retrospective on held-out structures; no prediction has been tested experimentally.

**No comparison with published baselines.** The arms here are compared with each other under matched conditions, not with existing interaction-prediction or pocket-conditioned generative models.

**Acyclic ligands and cofactors are excluded**, which removes some genuine binders along with the cryoprotectants and buffers the filter targets. mmCIF-only entries are also lost.

## 5. Data and code availability

Splits are committed with SHA-256 digests, every data source declares its licence in machine-readable form, and each figure is written alongside a JSON file of the exact values plotted. The corpus records are regenerable from the pipeline; the build is resumable and records every exclusion.
